title: WHAT EZEKIEL'S VISION REALLY REPRESENTS
paragraphs: The sky did not open over a comfortable man.
Far from home. Far from the Temple. Far from everything familiar.

When the prophet Ezekiel first saw the vision that would shake generations, he was standing beside the Kebar Canal in Babylon (Ezekiel 1:1-3). Jerusalem was collapsing. God's people were scattered. National identity was shattered. The future looked hopeless.
Most people know Ezekiel's vision for its strange imagery.
A radiant figure surrounded by overwhelming glory.
For centuries people have debated what Ezekiel saw.
Still others have imagined supernatural technology.
Yet many miss the central truth entirely.
The vision is not primarily about creatures.
It is not primarily about wheels.
It is not primarily about mystery.
It is about the glory of God refusing to be confined.
The opening chapter of Ezekiel begins with words that immediately signal divine revelation:
He does not say he saw visions about God.
He says he saw visions of God.
The entire vision moves toward a single destination.
The four living creatures first capture our attention.
Later Ezekiel identifies them as cherubim (Ezekiel 10:20).
Throughout biblical symbolism these images communicate aspects of creation itself.
The vision presents all creation gathered around God's throne.
Everything moves according to His command.
These wheels move in every direction without turning.
Their rims are filled with eyes.
Ancient readers would immediately recognize what modern readers often overlook.
When hearts break in silence, God sees.
The wheels reveal a God whose sovereign rule extends everywhere.
The throne is not fixed to Jerusalem.
The throne is not trapped in a building.
The throne is not dependent on circumstances.
This would have been revolutionary for exiles.
Their greatest fear was not merely losing their homeland.
Their greatest fear was losing God's presence.
Ancient nations often believed gods were tied to territories.
If your nation fell, your god had been defeated.
But Ezekiel's vision destroys that assumption.
The God of Israel was not defeated by Babylon.
He was already present in Babylon.
He was already reigning over Babylon.
He was already ruling above Babylon.
The exiles had not been abandoned.
Then Ezekiel's eyes are drawn upward.
Upon the throne sits one who appears in human form.
God reveals Himself through imagery that points toward humanity.
Centuries later the invisible God would fully reveal Himself through Jesus Christ.
The throne Ezekiel saw ultimately points us toward Christ.
The glory Ezekiel witnessed ultimately finds its fullest revelation in Christ.
The divine King is not an abstract force.
He is the God who would one day step into history, take on flesh, bear scars, and redeem sinners.
This becomes even more breathtaking when we reach Ezekiel 1:28.

"זֶה מַרְאֵה דְּמוּת כְּבוֹד־יְהוָה"
(zeh mar'eh demut kevod-YHWH)
"This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD."
He piles up these terms because human language is collapsing under the weight of divine majesty.
The prophet is straining to communicate the incomprehensible.
Then he does the only thing a sinner can do when confronted with divine glory.
Modern culture often seeks spiritual experiences without surrender.
But genuine encounters with God's glory always humble human pride.
Throughout Scripture, whenever people truly encounter God's holiness, self-exaltation dies.
Peter says, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man."
The closer we come to God's glory, the less impressed we become with ourselves.
And that brings us to what Ezekiel's vision really represents.
It represents the absolute sovereignty of God.
It represents God's presence among the broken.
It represents God's rule over chaos.
It represents God's glory above earthly powers.
It represents heaven invading human despair.
Most importantly, it represents the reality that God's redemptive purposes continue even when everything appears lost.
The exiles thought the story was over.
God revealed that He was still writing.
That truth echoes through the entire Gospel.
Humanity's greatest scandal was not Babylon.
By every human measure, the story should have ended there.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:
At Calvary, God's glory and God's grace met.
The God Ezekiel saw enthroned above creation became the Savior who bled for creation.
The Holy One entered the mess.
The Judge stepped into the sentence.
That is why Ezekiel's vision ultimately points beyond itself.
The One who reigns over every circumstance.
The One who remains present when life falls apart.
The One whose glory cannot be confined by buildings, nations, failures, scandals, or broken dreams.
The One who still rewrites stories.
Maybe your own life feels like exile right now.
Maybe you wonder if God has forgotten where you are.
And Christ is still rewriting stories.
What part of your life needs Christ to rewrite?
The throne you fear is empty is the very throne already ruling over the storm.
